Lessons.Title: Using Function Notation to Describe Rules (Part 1)
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning objective: express an input-output rule with function notation, evaluate it for permitted inputs, and reverse the process to find inputs for a specified output. Original Edulytiks adaptation of Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition Unit 4 Lesson 4, https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/4/4/preparation.html (CC BY 4.0). The source explicitly progresses from statements at specific values to generalized rules such as f(x)=3x−10.

Original first-party numeric rule: a service credit account starts at $25 and charges $3 for each booked appointment, so B(n)=25−3n dollars for whole n≥0 while the balance remains nonnegative. B(0)=25, B(2)=19, B(5)=10. To find when B(n)=7, solve 25−3n=7 -> n=6. Negative n or fractional booked appointments are outside the scenario, although algebraic function rule can be considered on real numbers in abstraction.
Translate a verbal rule 'multiply input by 3 then subtract 10' into f(x)=3x−10, with f(4)=2 and f(x)=11 at x=7. Demonstrate why f(x) names the rule at arbitrary input and f(4) is a particular output.

Student task: write generalized symbolic rules from two different verbal instructions, evaluate a table of input-output pairs and solve one equation from a known function output, checking domains. Teacher-scored rubric 0–2 for correct function rule, correct evaluation and reverse-solving, contextual/domain interpretation and explanation of equivalence between tables and equations.

KeyConcepts.Title: General function rule
KeyConcepts.Definition: f(x)=expression defines the output in terms of an arbitrary permitted x.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Keep named function and input variable distinct.

KeyConcepts.Title: Evaluation
KeyConcepts.Definition: Substituting the input into the function gives an output.

KeyConcepts.Title: Reverse solving
KeyConcepts.Definition: Knowing an output can produce an equation in the input.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Apply inverse operations and original domain.

WorkedExamples.Title: Generalize a verbal rule
WorkedExamples.Question: Multiply input by3 then subtract10. Write function and evaluate x=4.
WorkedExamples.Method: Represent the function with its stated input/output domain and verify the mathematical assertion.
Steps: Let x be any real input.
WorkedExamples.Check: Both verbal stages used in correct order.

WorkedExamples.Title: Recover an input
WorkedExamples.Question: Solve f(x)=11 for f(x)=3x−10.
WorkedExamples.Method: Represent the function with its stated input/output domain and verify the mathematical assertion.

WorkedExamples.Title: Model a balance function
WorkedExamples.Question: When is B(n)=7 for B(n)=25−3n?
WorkedExamples.Method: Represent the function with its stated input/output domain and verify the mathematical assertion.
Steps: Six is a nonnegative whole number and meaningful.
WorkedExamples.Check: Context domain and original equation both satisfied.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: One is a general rule and one is a particular value.
A real solution may represent fractional or negative item count.

SummaryPoints: Function notation expresses both general rules and particular output values.
Verbal sequences translate into ordered algebraic operations.
Solve f(x)=c to find valid inputs and check them.
Teacher reviews symbolic meaning and model interpretation.
